newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook - Gas oil depressed by arbitrage.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook - Gas oil depressed by arbitrage.

text.p: Singapore oil product prices are likely to see more losses in the week ahead with unsold supplies weighing on an already weak market, traders said on Monday.
After the awards of the Indian tender, gasoil prices nudged higher late last week but traders say levels may slip this week with arbitrage cargoes expected to sail east.
India bought 855,000 tonnes in 19 cargoes in its July tender, higher than traders initial expectations of between 400,000 tonnes and 600,000 tonnes.
But a depressed Mediterranean has opened the arbitrage window to the East. Traders said they expect as many as seven to eight long range (LR) vessels due for arrival in the east end June/early July.
They said the spread between the two regions was at just less than $30 per tonne based on Singapore June swaps value.
Optimistic sellers said there was still a chance cargoes might be diverted elsewhere if stocks in Singapore remained high.
Large volumes of arbitrage shipments during March/April, amounting to three million tonnes remained unsold, they said.

Meanwhile Chinese imports were limited. Chinese buyers were relying on domestic inventories to satisfy demand, traders said. A clamp down on smuggling into South China has contributed to the slow down in imports, they said.
Jet fuel prices staged a remarkable recovery on Friday but traders said the recovery may be shortlived as the downside momentum is stronger amid a weak market. Traders said demand is still weak.
The gasoline market was expected to fall before it recovers, traders said. They said there were ample supplies, with June cargoes from Australia, Thailand, South Korea and Yanbu expected.
Regional demand was limited to India, which cancelled a tender for June 10-14 delivery to Bombay and re-issued it for June 18-22 deliveries.
Traders said they were looking to Taiwan's import tender for July, which closes June 4, and for a price fall in Asia to open the arbitrage window to the U.S. and soak up some length.

Sellers were also pinning their hopes on U.S. demand to remove some supply, although a seasonal surge in demand in China and South Korea was likely to reduce some surplus supply over the next four weeks.
In the naptha market, the contango in the Singapore market for June and July barrels was expected to revert to backwardation, reflecting Japan's open-specification market for August and September.
Traders said petrochemical plants in South Korea were returning from turnarounds though refineries were still in the midst of their own shutdowns.

In fuel oil, the 180-cst grade high sulphur market was expected to be supported at above the $100-per-tonne level after a local trader emerged to bid for a June cargo late last last week, traders said.
The local trader has bought at least five cargoes in the past two weeks, seen as routine demand, and his buying interest would support sentiment, they said.

Traders said a fire at a residue hydro-sulphuriser unit at Taiwan's 200,000 bpd Taoyuan refinery has no immediate impact on fuel oil prices. The unit is used to reduce the sulphur content of fuel oil.
